A hot air balloon $B$ is flying horizontally to the observer $O$ at a constant height of $300\,\text{m}$ above the ground. The angle of elevation $\theta $ made by the balloon and an observer is increasing at a rate of $0.05$ radians per second. What is the speed of the balloon when $\theta =\frac{\pi }{6}?$
question.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14212968/assets/813a4a253bdac3c44fe66da2728ad01bf3f1db2e0612093ce8f6a81b60e50161.png)

In the figure, $y$ is the altitude of the hot air balloon, and $x$ is the horizontal distance between the balloon and the observer. The quantity $y=300\,\text{m}$ does not change with time because the hot air balloon stays at a constant altitude.

We wish to calculate $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ To do this, let's start by setting up a relation between $x$ and $y.$ Relative to the angle $\theta ,$ the sides $x$ and $y$ are the adjacent and opposite, respectively. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta  & =\frac{y}{x} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta  & =\frac{300}{x} \\ x & =300\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(300\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta ) \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-300{csc}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot \frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the given information, we have $\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}=0.05$ and $\theta =\frac{\pi }{6}.$ Substituting these values into the above, we reach

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-300{csc}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})(0.05) \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-300(2)^{2}(0.05) \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-60.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the speed of the hot air balloon is $60\,\text{m/s}.$
